newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldovan nationalist backs president in run-off.
newsitem.headline: Moldovan nationalist backs president in run-off.

text.p: Nationalist Valeriu Matei, who won nine percent of the vote in the first round of Moldova's presidential elections, urged his supporters on Friday to back President Mircea Snegur in the run-off on December 1.
"I call on you, dear voters, to back candidate Mircea Snegur on December 1," Matei said in an appeal on radio and television.
Snegur, who won last Sunday's first round with 39 percent, will face a strong challenge in the run-off from Parliament Chairman Petru Lucinschi, who polled 28 percent.

Pro-Romanian Matei, who heads the Party of Democratic Forces, said he had decided to back the incumbent president, because "antinational and antidemocratic forces grouping around Lucinschi oblige us to react properly".
Two other former candidates, Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli with nine percent of votes and Communist Party leader Vladimir Voronin with 10 percent, have already backed Lucinschi.
Snegur had called for "a joint front against revanchists and communists" and Matei was his only remaining possible ally.
Four other ex-candidates got two percent of the vote or less, and analysts say Snegur and Lucinschi are evenly matched before the run-off.
The two men, both 56 and senior Communist Party leaders in Soviet times, have different visions of the future for Moldova, a landlocked state of 4.3 million between Romania and Ukraine.

Centre-right Snegur, backed by his Party of Revival and Harmony in alliance with a group of minor nationalist parties, wants closer ties with the West and Romania, with which Moldova shares common language, history and culture.
Snegur has repeatedly said the "corrupt and incompetent" government must go. He wants to change the constitution to boost his powers and turn Moldova into a presidential republic.
Sangheli said on Wednesday night his cabinet would resign once the new president had been elected "to preserve civil peace and order in the republic".
Left-leaning Lucinschi, who was the leader of the Communist Party of Soviet Moldova, does not intend to change the law.
He seeks equally close ties with Romania and regional power Russia, on which Moldova heavily depends for energy and fuel.
Analysts say Snegur may be more popular in villages, whereas Lucinschi could get more support in towns and from ethnic minorities, who make up 35 percent of the population.
